Maladaptive Strategies.value: control eating strictly to feel in control
I imagine getting revenge on the people responsible
go along with whatever others want to feel safe

Threat.value: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger

Memory.value: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel isolated and set apart from others
I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

vignette:
Rohan, a 41-year-old park ranger, sits with a stillness that seems at odds with the tension in his shoulders. It has been eighteen months since the solo trekking trip that he now refers to only as "that time." He had been hiking in a remote mountain range, an experienced outdoorsman seeking solitude, when he was taken by a local militia. They mistook him for a foreign operative. The memory of it doesn't arrive as a continuous narrative, but as a slideshow of stark, silent images: the rough texture of the burlap sack pulled over his head, the worn-out insignia on a soldier's uniform, the specific crack in the ceiling of the room where they held him. Sometimes, when he tries to recall the sequence of events, he feels nothing at all, a profound numbness that makes him feel like he’s recounting a story about a stranger.

His captors wore uniforms, and now the sight of any official attire—a police officer at a traffic stop, a security guard at the mall, even his own crisp National Park Service uniform—sends a jolt of ice through him. At work, in the vast wilderness he once considered his sanctuary, he feels constantly exposed. He has come to believe that the park visitors are watching him, judging his every move, their gazes a silent accusation. This feeling of being seen is a direct echo of the interrogation room, where he was forced to stand for hours under the unblinking stare of his captors. He is certain that a stronger, smarter person would never have been so naive as to hike in that region alone; this self-reproach is a constant, quiet hum beneath his daily thoughts. What happened feels less like a misfortune and more like a permanent stain of humiliation he can never wash away.

In the months after his release, Rohan’s life began to shrink. He developed habits he didn't understand at first. To regain a sense of control that was stripped from him, he began to restrict his eating with rigid precision, weighing every portion and counting every calorie. The gnawing hunger was a feeling he could command, unlike the terror. At night, when sleep wouldn't come, he would lie awake and construct elaborate revenge fantasies, imagining himself powerful and his captors helpless. These thoughts provided a fleeting surge of strength but left him exhausted and agitated by morning. With his partner and his colleagues, he found himself becoming excessively agreeable, nodding along to any suggestion and suppressing his own needs. It felt safer to be compliant, to offer no resistance, to simply go along with whatever others wanted. He just wanted to feel safe, and he could no longer trust that he was, even when his partner held him and told him he was home.

His body remembers the trauma in ways his mind sometimes doesn't. A few weeks ago, while on patrol, a deer suddenly bolted from the undergrowth. Rohan didn't just jump; he dropped to the ground, his heart hammering against his ribs as if he were under attack. When a memory-image of a guard’s face flashes into his mind, he often feels a ghost of a sharp, radiating pain in his side, right where a boot once connected. These moments are disorienting, visceral intrusions that make the past feel terrifyingly present. He feels utterly set apart from everyone he knows, isolated by an experience he cannot adequately explain and which they could never truly understand.

It was an incident at the park’s visitor center that finally compelled him to seek help. A tourist, a veteran wearing a military-style jacket, began asking him detailed questions about patrol routes and park security. Rohan froze, the man’s authoritative tone transporting him back to the interrogation room. He felt the floor tilt beneath him, the sounds of the center fading into a dull roar. He was there, and he was here, and the terror was absolute. He managed to excuse himself, but the episode left him shaken for days. He is terrified of losing his job, the one piece of his old life he has clung to. More than that, he is afraid that this broken, watchful version of himself is all he will ever be.
